title: Model: Energy from Sun to Plants and Animals

opener.title: Model: Energy from Sun to Plants and Animals
opener.question: How can a few boxes and arrows show the way energy moves from the sun through a whole community of living things?
opener.alt: An opening film that starts on the Arctic seen from space, then zooms to the Barents Sea, to Bear Island, to its seabird cliffs, to puffins on a rock, and finally to an arctic fox.

k-warmup.text: Look at the rabbit and the clover. Turn the arrow so it points the way you think a food chain arrow should go. Then pick what your arrow stands for, tap Save, and write your reasons. You will check it in Part 4.

k-words.text: Model. Producer. Consumer. Food chain. Food web. Decomposer.

k-part1.text: Charles Elton printed this page in nineteen twenty-seven. Tap each yellow line to read it in plain English. Then trace his arrows on the Bear Island diagram, from the sea to the polar bear, and from the plants to the arctic fox.

k-quiz.text: Three quick questions, just for you. They are not graded. Tap an answer and read the note under it. For each one, ask yourself which way the energy moves.

k-assign.text: Now add your half of page eighteen. Answer the two Part B questions about your model. In Part C, write your notebook page. Then tap evidence cards in the planner to build your C-E-R about how energy moves from the sun.

wordlens.intro: Tap a word to see what it means. You met some of these yesterday.

words.def: A simple picture or object that shows how something works. Every model leaves some details out.
A living thing that makes its own food from sunlight. Plants are producers.
A living thing that gets energy by eating other living things.
One path of energy from the sun to a plant to the animals that eat it.
Many food chains linked together. It shows that most animals eat more than one thing.
A living thing, like a mushroom or worm, that breaks down dead plants and animals.

source.title: Charles Elton's own words
source.alt: Two printed pages from the 1927 book Animal Ecology. The left page, page 56, is text about animals and their food. The right page, page 58, has two diagrams of boxes joined by many arrows.
source.intro: In the summer of 1921, Charles Elton, a 21-year-old student from Oxford University in England, sailed to Bear Island in the Arctic. He wrote down which animals ate which. Two years later, he and a plant scientist named Victor Summerhayes turned those notes into a diagram. In 1927, Elton put it in his book Animal Ecology. Here are two of its pages.
job: Tap each yellow line to read it in plain English.
Then find the two lines in the hunts.

lines.en: Animals spend most of their lives eating. What drives every animal is finding the right kind of food, and enough of it.
In the end, every animal depends on plants for its energy. Only plants can turn sunlight and simple chemicals into food that animals can eat.
Plant-eaters are hunted by meat-eaters. The meat-eaters get the sun's energy third-hand. Then other meat-eaters may hunt them, until you reach an animal that nothing hunts.
So animals are linked in chains by food, and every chain leads back to plants. We call these food-chains. All the food-chains in one place, together, we call the food-cycle.
The food-cycle on Bear Island, a bare spot in the Arctic. Dotted lines are food links that were likely but not proved yet. To read it, start at 'marine animals' and follow the arrows.

asks.q: Hunt 1: Find the line where Elton gives the name “food-chains.”
asks.yes: Yes. Elton is one of the scientists who made the words food chain famous.
asks.no: Not that one. Look near the bottom of the left page.

asks.q: Hunt 2: Find the line that says where ALL animals get their energy in the end.
asks.yes: Yes. From plants, which turn sunlight into food.
asks.no: Not quite. Look for the line about sunlight on the left page.

source.credit: Source: Charles S. Elton, Animal Ecology (1927), pages 56 and 58. Scan from the Internet Archive (public domain in the U.S.). Fig. 4 first appeared in Summerhayes and Elton (1923). Plain-English version written for this lesson.

trace.title: Trace a path on Elton's diagram
trace.intro: Here is Elton's Bear Island diagram, bigger. Each box is a living thing (or something like dung). Each arrow shows food, and the energy in it, moving to an eater. Tap the boxes in order to trace a path.
trace.alt: Elton's 1923 Bear Island diagram: about forty boxes with names like Plants, Ptarmigan, Arctic Fox, Seals, Polar Bear, Marine Animals, Dung and Bacteria, joined by many arrows.

paths.q: Start at Marine animals (sea creatures). Follow the arrows to the polar bear.
paths.start: Elton says to start at Marine animals. Find that box on the right side.
paths.hint: Follow the arrow that leaves your last box. Which box does its head touch?
paths.win: Marine animals → seals → polar bear. A food chain that starts in the sea.

paths.q: Now start at Plants, on the left. Follow the arrows through a bird to the arctic fox.
paths.start: Find the box that says PLANTS, on the left side.
paths.hint: Follow an arrow from your last box to a bird, then on to the fox.
paths.win: Plants → ptarmigan → arctic fox. A second chain, from the land.

find.q: Find 3 more boxes with an arrow pointing INTO the arctic fox.

says.seals: Seal meat, often left over by polar bears.

find.hint: Look for arrows whose heads touch the ARCTIC FOX box. Which boxes do they come from?
find.win: The arctic fox eats at least five different things. One neat chain can't show that, so Elton drew a web.

trace.wow: Elton and Summerhayes drew this in 1923 from what they saw on the island. It is one of the first food diagrams ever drawn, and it is not a neat chain. It is a tangled web, with dead plants, dung, and bacteria in it too.
trace.credit: Diagram: Fig. 4 in Charles S. Elton, Animal Ecology (1927), from Summerhayes and Elton (1923). Internet Archive scan (public domain in the U.S.).

flip.intro: A classmate drew this food chain, but two arrows point the wrong way. Run it first and see what the model says. Then fix it.
job: Tap ▶ Run the energy and read what each arrow says.
Tap an arrow to flip it.
Run it again until every arrow tells the truth.

yes: Energy goes from the sun to the grass. True: grass catches sunlight and makes food.
Energy goes from the grass to the cricket. True: crickets eat grass.
Energy goes from the cricket to the frog. True: frogs eat crickets.
Energy goes from the frog to the hawk. True: hawks eat frogs.
no: This arrow says the grass gives its energy to the sun. The sun doesn't eat grass!
This arrow says the cricket feeds the grass. Grass doesn't eat crickets!
This arrow says the frog feeds the cricket. Crickets don't eat frogs!
This arrow says the hawk feeds the frog. Frogs don't eat hawks!
flip.tryAgain: {n} arrow(s) still point backward. Tap a red arrow to flip it, then run the energy again.
flip.win: Every arrow points from the food to the eater, so the energy runs one way: from the sun to the hawk. At each link, some of the energy leaves as heat.

spots.text: Lily pads and other water plants. They catch sunlight and make their own food, just like algae. Apple snails eat them too.
Eastern mosquitofish, about as long as your finger, swarm in shallow water. They eat algae and tiny animals.
A great egret waits at the edge of the grass, then spears small fish with its sharp bill.
A largemouth bass hides in deeper water. It eats smaller fish, like mosquitofish.
American alligators eat fish, snails, turtles, and birds. Young alligators eat lots of snails.
These stalks are dead. Fungi and bacteria, mostly too small to see, are breaking them down. They are decomposers, and a simple food chain leaves them out.

pond.webNote: Look at the model: some living things now have two or more arrows coming in or going out. One chain can't show that. It's turning into a food web.
pond.win: Your model is a food web now. The apple snail eats algae AND water plants. The alligator eats snails AND fish. A food chain shows just one path through this web.
pond.key: Orange arrows: energy goes to (from the food to the eater). Dashed brown arrows: when it dies, decomposers break it down.

twist.quote: We refer to these as ‘food-chains,’ and to all the food-chains in a community as the ‘food-cycle.’
twist.alt: The top-left corner of Elton's diagram: boxes for Nitrogen, Protozoa, Bacteria, Dung, Mineral Salts, Dead Plants and Plants, joined by arrows in a loop.
twist.cap: Elton's loop: dung → bacteria → mineral salts → plants.
twist.line: Elton called his whole diagram a food-cycle, and it really has a loop in it: dung → bacteria → mineral salts → plants. But what goes around that loop is matter, the stuff living things are made of. Energy never loops. At every link some of it leaves as heat, so plants need new sunlight every single day. Matter cycles. Energy flows one way.
twist.chain: 📓 Next week starts page 19: how the organs in your body work together.

planner.title: Plan before you write
planner.intro: Tap two or more pieces of evidence to add them to your Evidence box. Then write your claim and reasoning in your own words.
cards: In my Part 4 model, every arrow points from the food to the eater.
Clover → rabbit: the clover makes food from sunlight, and the rabbit eats the clover.
Elton's Bear Island diagram traces plants → ptarmigan → arctic fox.
When two arrows pointed backward, the model said the frog fed the cricket, which is not true.
The alligator eats snails and fish, so it needs two arrows coming in. That makes a food web.
At every link, some energy leaves as heat, so less reaches each animal up the chain.

checklist: Warm-Up: your arrow prediction and two sentences of reasons.
Part B: questions 1 and 2, in complete sentences.
Part C: your notebook page (both boxes).
C-E-R: a claim, at least two links from your model as evidence, and your reasoning about the arrows.

data.title: Where the energy went in a Florida spring
data.unit: kilocalories per square meter in a year
data.ylabel: Energy (kilocalories per square meter per year)
data.intro: In the 1950s, a scientist named Howard T. Odum measured the energy in Silver Springs, a clear spring in central Florida. He measured how much energy each group of living things took in during one year.
job: Drag across the bars to read each number.
Find the smallest bar. Can you even see it?
data.ask: Which took in MORE energy: the decomposers, or all the meat-eaters and top meat-eaters put together?

opts.hint: Add the two meat-eater bars: 383 + 21. Then compare with the decomposers.
Read the decomposer bar, then add 383 + 21. Are they close?

data.win: Decomposers: 5,060. All the meat-eaters together: 383 + 21 = 404. The decomposers took in more than 12 times as much, and a simple food chain leaves them out completely.
data.alt: A bar graph of energy taken in during one year at Silver Springs, Florida: plants and algae 20,810; plant-eaters 3,368; meat-eaters 383; top meat-eaters 21; decomposers 5,060 kilocalories per square meter.
data.credit: Data: H. T. Odum (1957), “Trophic structure and productivity of Silver Springs, Florida,” Ecological Monographs 27: 55–112, as shown in OpenStax Biology 2e, “Energy Flow through Ecosystems.” Values are kilocalories per square meter per year.

cabinet.title: A seal skull more than 14 million years old
cabinet.alt: A 3D scan of a small, brown fossil seal skull with large eye openings and a few teeth.
cabinet.text: This is a real fossil skull of Leptophoca lenis, a small seal, from the Smithsonian. It was found in Calvert County, Maryland, in rock that formed under a warm sea more than 14 million years ago. Seals are on Elton's page: marine animals → seals → polar bear. This seal probably ate fish, and bigger animals may have eaten it. When it died, decomposers broke down everything except its bones.
cabinet.credit: 3D model: Leptophoca lenis True, skull (USNM PAL 347348), Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Department of Paleobiology. CC0.
